speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My response will also cover the matters raised in the question by Mr Leong Mun Wai, which is for written reply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the Mah Kiat Seng case, the High Court made a number of observations about the conduct of a specific Police officer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The officer had detained a person under section 7 of the Mental Health (Care & Treatment) Act (MHCTA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The subject was believed to be dangerous by reason of mental disorder.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was reported to have suddenly touched the head of a stranger's four-year-old child, without having any reason to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was also observed to have behaved erratically.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, it was the child's mother who gave the report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are studying the judgment in this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since an appeal may be filed, we usually refrain from commenting in detail on Court decisions – unless it is in the public interest that we do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Administration of Justice (Protection) Act provides for statements on pending Court proceedings to be made, in such situations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In our view, this is one such case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But nevertheless, I will be careful in what I say, and will be quite constrained and circumscribed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before I comment on the case itself, let me give Members some perspective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, we are one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our level of safety and security is underpinned by the high levels of trust between the Government and the public, and a system of policing that is highly trusted and effective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the 2022 Gallup Law and Order Survey, 95% of Singapore residents said they felt safe walking alone on the streets at night.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Singapore Police Force (SPF)'s Public Perception Survey in 2021 showed that public trust in the SPF is at 96%.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the same survey, 98% of respondents said that they would provide assistance and information to the Police, if there was a need.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This would not be possible without the high levels of trust in, and competence of, the Singapore Police Force, built up over the years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you compare it with countries where they want to abolish the Police, first world countries, you can see the contrast.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The framework we have in place, to ensure that our officers behave in accordance with the law, has helped to maintain standards and trust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will mention the following: First, the Police themselves are the first layer of check; there is a process to investigate any abuse of power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we ourselves take action against errant officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Officers' actions can be assessed and actions taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, where necessary, we can convene – and we have convened – the Independent Review Panel (IRP).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The IRP consists of former judges, former senior public officers and other individuals with significant standing in society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It provides an independent assessment on whether the internal investigations were fair and thorough.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And third, if criminal offences are potentially disclosed, we recommend Court prosecution and let the Courts deal with the matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts thus provide a third layer of safeguards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The supervision of the Courts is an integral part of ensuring that our system functions properly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And about 10 Police officers have been charged in court each year, for the past three years, for criminal offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will not hesitate to take action when there is an infraction – that is essential to maintain trust with the public and discipline within the Force.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, while we have to be strict about upholding the highest standards for Police, we have to ensure that our analysis of officers' ground judgments is reasonable and fair.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police officers work in high-stress and dynamic environments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They often have to make split-second decisions and take decisive action, based on the limited information that they have.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would not be realistic to critique their every move with the benefit of hindsight, removed from the conditions on the ground.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The officers must be given sufficient latitude to make swift ground assessments and decisions, as long as they have acted in good faith.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An environment in which Police actions are unfairly critiqued, will inevitably undermine public trust in the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will also lead to defensive policing – where the ground officers will try to do the least possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will fear that everything they do will be over-analysed and picked apart unfairly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would be easier in such situations to not do anything.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Defensive policing is, essentially, no policing – and that can have a detrimental effect on our safety and security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And an unfair characterisation of the Force will eventually also lead to the public thinking of the Police as the enemy and viewing the Police with suspicion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have so far avoided that situation and we have to be careful to avoid that outcome.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the specifics of this case, we do have some concerns about the judgment that has been delivered, in this respect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court found that the detained subject had "unusual" behaviour, but those did not qualify as symptoms of someone with a mental disorder.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Police officer was just equally observing and had to make decisions on the ground.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court also said that the officer took a dislike to the detained person and that the officer had made up observations about him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are looking closely at the Court's reasons for reaching these conclusions – the Police tell me that they take a different view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In deciding what to do, we have to bear in mind that decisions in individual cases – Court decisions – can have a much larger and unintended effect, of negatively impacting how officers react in future to such situations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court also made some comments about several issues in law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such as what the word "danger" in the MHCTA must entail, on the ground.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And whether the powers for the Police to "apprehend" someone under the MHCTA and to "arrest" someone under the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) are the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we reach the conclusion that the Court's findings are in fact – as advised by AGC – reasonable and correct, then we will have to internalise that, and make sure the key points are made clear to our officers, so that they understand the situation better.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Right now, the sense amongst the Police officers is one of concern, on what liability may befall them, for actions which they may take in the discharge of their duties.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I definitely concur that Singaporeans have high trust in the Police force and a Police officer on ground need to have the latitude in carrying out their duty.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: One, can I just clarify if all the patrol officers on the ground are wearing the wearable CCTV, the cameras, throughout the whole force?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Second, the Minister said that a few of the Police officers were charged in Court for criminal offence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Were they charged in the course of their duty or their own behaviour which caused them to be charged in Court?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point I am making is that the fact that they are Police officers, gives no immunity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they have committed an offence and we investigate and we find that there is a prima facie case, where AGC believes that it can be proven beyond reasonable doubt, then they will be charged.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is probably on the on the flip side.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have a resident who came to me recently about the case of her husband who, supposedly, has a mental disorder.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When he was violent towards her, the Police could not take action against him.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is, if the Minister can share, what processes could be made to be clearer to the ground officers in cases involving mental disorder, especially as what you mentioned just now, the risk of defensive policy to the ground officers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My suggestion is possibly, if there could be further link-up between officers dealing with mental capacity cases and IMH, and whether there be could be quicker relations, with regard to individuals with mental disorders?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the Mah Kiat Seng case, the person's behaviour was observed to be erratic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, the judge accepted that there was some of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But IMH felt that he was not mentally insane; and that is entirely possible; there is a wide continuum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise, I will have to look at the facts of the case that you referred to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a bit difficult to answer here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is entirely possible that one can exhibit various degrees of bizarre behaviour without actually being classified as insane by IMH.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the wife might well consider the husband to be mentally unsound, but the husband may not qualify in the facts of your case to be classified as unsound.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not have to be physical assault, but if there is a risk, then there are possibilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well before that, the person who came to see you, can be assisted to seek Protection Orders from the Courts as well.
